q: How is the fur actually rendered?
a:
The best primary evidence is a description of FurMark's rendering as heavily multipass, with about 100 passes, where each pass runs a GLSL vertex and pixel shader that makes the hairs progressively finer, with two dynamic lights giving self-shadowing 12. That is the classic "shell" or layered fur method: draw the mesh repeatedly, pushing each shell outward by a growing fur length. A well-known general write-up of shell texturing describes exactly that approach, though it uses HLSL, not GLSL 3.

What I could not find is a dedicated oZone3D or Geeks3D tutorial for FurMark's fur shader. oZone3D's tutorial index lists GLSL topics such as fog and texturing but nothing on fur 4. So the "100 passes" and "shell" wording rests on a secondary description of FurMark, not on a JeGX source; it is consistent with, but not proven by, the developer's own text. Not confirmed from a primary source.

What the developer does say: version 1.8.0 added a vertex displacement mapping effect that "controls the height of fur", so some parts of the torus have very short fur 5. Version 1.9.0 (25 Feb 2011) added a dynamic background and a mode with two interlaced furry tori and a moving camera 6. The 1.6.0 post (7 Jan 2009) added a post-processing pass whose shader loads from post-processing-fx.xml so users could write their own effect in GLSL 7.

q: What are the presets and burn-in modes, and how is the score calculated?
a:
Presets. Version 1.9.0 introduced two presets that can submit online scores: Preset:1080 (1920x1080 fullscreen, no AA, post FX off, dynamic background, burn-in on) and Preset:720 (1280x720, same settings) 6. Version 1.16.0 (the changelog dates it 2014-06-25; the post is 26 June 2015) added P1440 (QHD) and P2160 (4K/UHD) presets, with Top-20 tables for 1080, 1440 and 2160 8.

Modes. The command-line reference from November 2008 already documents a "run_mode": 1 for benchmark and 2 for stability test, a default benchmark length of 60,000 ms (/max_time), a frame cap (/max_frames) and /xtreme_burning, "a mode that overburns the GPU" 9. So Xtreme burn-in predates 1.9.0 by more than two years. (I had said earlier that 1.9.0 introduced it; the 2008 reference shows that is wrong.)

The score. The developer gives paired numbers: a GTX 480 scored 6478 points (108 FPS) in FurMark 1.8.2 at 1080p, and 1769 points (29 FPS) in 1.9.0 6. Dividing, 6478 / 108 = 60.0 and 1769 / 29 = 61.0, matching the 60-second default run. So the score is, to rounding, the number of frames rendered during the 60-second benchmark, i.e. average FPS x 60. That is my inference from the developer's own figures, not a stated formula; no document I found spells it out. It also explains why 1.9.0 scores are far lower than 1.8.2 scores: the heavier workload cut FPS by about 3.7x 6.

q: What is GeeXLab, and how did it shape FurMark 2?
a:
GeeXLab is Geeks3D's cross-platform scripting tool for 3D programming, demos and creative coding, with Lua and Python as main languages and GLSL for OpenGL and Vulkan 10. Its lineage is documented by JeGX himself in December 2015: the first public GeeXLab appeared "around 6 years" earlier (so about 2009); GLSL Hacker, "a heavily revamped version", had its first public version in January 2013; and in December 2015 GLSL Hacker was renamed back to GeeXLab when Direct3D 12 support arrived 11. The current release in my sources is 0.67.0 (5 October 2026), for Windows and Linux on x86-64 and arm64 10.

FurMark 2 is built on it. The 24 Feb 2024 release post says FurMark 2 is built with GeeXLab: the GUI is a pure GeeXLab application and the furmark command-line tool is built with the GeeXLab SDK, which is why it is cross-platform 12. The changelog repeatedly lists "updated with GeeXLab" library versions (for example 0.49.3 in FurMark 2.0.4.0 and 0.60.x in 2.3.0.0) 13. The exact first-release date of the original GeeXLab is "about 2009" by the author's own estimate; I found no dated release post.

q: Has FurMark verifiably damaged a graphics card?
a:
I found no controlled test, teardown or RMA confirmation proving FurMark alone killed a card. What exists:

  • A documented hardware weakness. Geeks3D's own 2009 post says the Radeon HD 4850/4870 VRM was undersized for FurMark/OCCT loads, which is why AMD added driver protection 14. That is the developer admitting the risk was real for that generation.
  • A vendor-acknowledged risk for other parts. A review quoted by Geeks3D said that, at an end-user level, FurMark and OCCT "really can be dangerous" because they can draw too much power from the PSU, even though cards can no longer be toasted by them 15.
  • Forum anecdotes, not proof. HardForum and Overclock.net threads describe dead HD 4870-class cards after FurMark; the same threads include replies attributing the failures to overclocking, poor cooling, or a card that was already failing 16.

Conclusion: plausible on old, undersized VRMs, not demonstrated as a verified cause. Practical third-party guides recommend conservative run lengths and temperature monitoring 17; I did not establish a specific run-length recommendation directly from the developer.

q: Do modern GPUs still detect or limit FurMark?
a:
Power limiting is now routine, but whether drivers still detect FurMark by name is not established.

  • Hardware and BIOS limits are real. Tom's Hardware measured the RX 7900 XTX at 366 W in FurMark at 1440p and wrote that "AMD's new cards throttle more than just about any other GPU we've tested recently", calling FurMark an atypical worst-case load 18.
  • Name detection. In 2009 the developer shipped a copy of FurMark renamed etqw.exe (Enemy Territory: Quake Wars) specifically to get game profiles and to bypass "the FurMark detection included in the Catalyst graphics driver" 7. That is first-party confirmation of the early check, and of the rename trick, from FurMark's own author.
  • Today. Forum posts disagree: one says Nvidia detects FurMark, a reply says it does not and that the lower state comes from a power-limit "perf cap" reason; another says the card BIOS does the throttling 19. I found no Nvidia or AMD document stating that a current driver detects FurMark. Not confirmed.
  • An RTX 4090 anecdote: a Linus Tech Tips post reports FurMark staying near 67% of TDP, while a reply says a power virus should still push over 400 W 19. Treat as anecdote.

q: What did FurMark 1.9.0 and the Xtreme burning mode change?
a:
1.9.0 (25 February 2011, per KitGuru quoting JeGX) kept FurMark an OpenGL 2.0 stress test covering GeForce 6 to GTX 500, Radeon HD 2000 to HD 6000 and Intel HD 2000/3000. It made the workload heavier to track recent cards (GTX 480: 6478 points at 108 FPS in 1.8.2, 1769 points at 29 FPS in 1.9.0), added a dynamic background (optional), a two-torus mode, and the two online-score presets 6. The timing matters: it arrived weeks after the January 2011 limiter debate 20.

Xtreme burning is older (see Q2). The overclockers.com thread title for 1.9.0 is "The Return of the Furry Donut" 21. A forum poster in my sources says a good FPS without Xtreme burn-in is around 30, and around 15 with it, depending on the card. That is one user, not a developer figure 22.

q: Who is JeGX, and what else did Geeks3D and oZone3D build?
a:
A 2012 article says GPU Caps Viewer is developed by Jérôme "JeGX" Guinot, based in Switzerland, who calls himself an "OpenGL developer and GPU torturer"; it also says he owns Geeks3D and founded oZone3D.Net, and lists his creations as GeeXLab, FurMark, TessMark, FluidMark, ShaderToyMark, GPU Shark, GLinspector, EVGA OC Scanner and MSI Kombustor 23. That is secondary; I found no formal biography or interview.

Primary traces: JeGX's 2007 post on oZone3D announces GPU Caps Viewer, describing a "GPU-Burner" that opens many 3D windows, each rendering a GLSL toon-shaded object (the forerunner of FurMark-style burning) 24. A 2008 release note credits the GPU burner to the FurMark engine 25. He is still updating GPU Caps Viewer: version 1.64 appeared in March 2025 and he wrote there is no 2.0 planned but he will "try to update GPU Caps Viewer 1.64.x as long as I can" 25. GPU Shark 2.11 appeared in the recent-posts list of Geeks3D in November 2026 26.

q: How does FurMark behave on Raspberry Pi and Arm?
a:
FurMark 2.3 (6 May 2024) added Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit (arm64/aarch64) support. JeGX wrote that on a Raspberry Pi 4 it runs at 1 FPS at 1024x640, and on the "a lot faster" Raspberry Pi 5 it reaches 4 FPS at that resolution. He disabled the preset benchmarks because the score-submission interface is not usable at those frame rates, and said he removed Raspberry Pi dependencies, hoping it works on other arm64 platforms 26. Later changelog entries monitor the Pi 5 GPU and fix the donut's colour in Vulkan on arm64 "visible on raspberry pi 5" 13. A Geeks3D forum thread reports flickering in the Vulkan arm build, which the developer attributes to rendering only the first two swapchain images 27.

Why was it added? The post gives no reason beyond cross-platform coverage; it follows from the GeeXLab engine already running on Raspberry Pi OS (GeeXLab 0.59 was released for Raspberry Pi OS) 26. The reason is inferred, not stated. I could not find Pi GPU temperature results.

q: How does FurMark compare with other stress tools?
a:
No independent lab comparison turned up; the guides I found are secondary, SEO-heavy and not consistent on numbers. Several guides characterise FurMark as an atypically intense thermal/power workload, OCCT as useful for error detection, and looped game-like benchmarks such as Heaven or Time Spy as complementary stability checks 28. Those descriptions do not establish a universal temperature or wattage ranking against every OCCT mode on every GPU. Tom's Hardware's choice is instructive: it measures real-world power with a looped game (Metro Exodus) and a FurMark run as a deliberate worst-case bracket 18.

The developer's own positioning is consistent: FurMark 2 is "a very intensive GPU stress test" and "also a graphics benchmark" 29. Specific heat and wattage comparisons would need a controlled test on one card; I did not find one and did not run one.

q: What do the online scores and comparative tables show?
a:
Geeks3D keeps a comparative score table (pages for 1920x1080, 1280x720, 1280x1024 and 3840x2160) with update entries as recent as 18 Nov 2022 for the RTX 4090 and Intel Arc A750/A380 30. For FurMark 2, Geeks3D publishes charts per preset and API (OpenGL and Vulkan): each GPU's score is the mean of all submitted scores with some outliers removed, only scores from FurMark 2.0.8 or later are used, GPUs with fewer than five unique scores get a grey bar, and the charts were last updated 10 November 2026 against a database version of 9 November 2026 31. There is also a 3440x1440 chart updated the same day 26.

How large the database is: I found no total submission count. Not confirmed. One third-party listing suggests an RTX 4090 result of 37,387 points (623 FPS) and an RX 6800 XT result of 18,035 points (301 FPS); both fit the roughly 60 points per FPS I derived in Q2, but that comes from a third-party score site and not Geeks3D 32.

q: Why fur, rather than explosions, fire or a game level?
a:
Confirmed: FurMark began as a fur-rendering benchmark. On 26 August 2007 creator JeGX wrote that he had released it four days earlier and highlighted how little the measured performance depended on CPU speed, and how much it loaded GPUs F1. Its name openly combines 'fur' and 'mark' (a benchmark mark). Later descriptions explain that its synthetic fur algorithm deliberately applies an unusually intensive graphics workload F2F3.

What makes fur an attractive technical showcase? A furry surface is not simply a flat material: it has thousands of visible tips or layers, translucency, directional shading and silhouette complexity. Classic real-time approaches can require repeated geometry draws, texture lookups and alpha blending. NVIDIA's February 2007 developer white paper explains the general graphics challenge and the shells-and-fins family of solutions F4. This explains how fur could make a stress-test subject, but does not independently prove every internal technique used by FurMark.

Why this exact creative choice? Unknown. I found no JeGX interview saying 'I chose fur instead of fire because …'. The documented goal was GPU-dominant stress, not an action scene; claiming a personal inspiration would be invention. Some versions later added fire-like visual effects, but fur remained the named workload.

q: Why a torus/doughnut rather than a furry animal—and did furry doughnuts already exist?
a:
Confirmed: The main object is a hair-covered torus, an endlessly continuous ring. A torus is a conventional procedural graphics test object because its curved inside, outside and silhouette show effects from many angles without requiring an animated character rig. That is a technical interpretation, not a direct quote from JeGX.

Importantly, FurMark did not invent the idea of the furry doughnut. A Stanford computer-graphics project from 2001 contains an explicitly labelled 'Furry Donut' example made with fur shaders F5. Earlier fur-rendering research also used torus-shaped models. This is evidence of a pre-existing graphics-demo motif, not proof JeGX saw or borrowed that particular project. The answer to 'which illustration or artist directly inspired JeGX?' is not established.

The ring makes the image striking and readable. Its memorable absurdity—the contrast between a fluffy toy-like shape and a stressed graphics card—is an interpretation of how its iconography works, rather than official lore.

q: What did the earliest doughnut look like, and how has it changed?
a:
Confirmed historical arc: The August 2007 report already presented this as a fur demo, with contemporary screenshot(s) and 8800 GTX temperature measurements F1. A 2 December 2008 illustrated contemporary article shows the familiar ring as the benchmark's visual centre, well before FurMark 2 F6. Early FurMark was fundamentally an OpenGL 2-era repeating fur scene.

Later releases changed more than hardware support. FurMark 1.8.0 (February 2010) introduced a post-process heat effect and displacement controlling fur height F7. FurMark 1.9.0 (February 2011) introduced an animated background, camera movement and a mode with two interlaced furry tori F8. FurMark 2 (public in February 2024) retained the iconic donut and added the knot scene F9. The continuity of the central fur-covered shape is documented, though exact colours and decorations vary by release, API, settings and screenshots.

Do not treat an image of today's FurMark 2 as a perfect reconstruction of the 2007 scene.

q: Are those hairs actual polygons or a shader trick?
a:
Partially established. Independent technical descriptions of classic FurMark refer to many shader passes and layered fur, sometimes characterised as roughly a hundred passes F10. There is not a publicly audited primary-source FurMark shader breakdown here proving that exact pass count, the shape of every strand or the implementation in FurMark 2. The previous technical Q&A makes that limitation explicit F11.

In the general shells and fins approach, a base shape is repeatedly drawn with increasingly displaced, partly transparent layers, sometimes augmented by fins at its outer edge; blending produces the impression of countless hairs without simulating every strand independently F4. Other graphics research used volumetric textures to avoid individually modelling hair F5. Explanation of the method is not proof of FurMark's proprietary shader.

What JeGX definitely documented was changing fur length by vertex displacement in 1.8.0 F7. Saying 'the doughnut contains millions of physically simulated individual hairs' would be unjustified.

q: Why does it just rotate, instead of moving through a fictional world?
a:
Confirmed: The original benchmark's purpose was repeatable, GPU-centred workload and temperature testing, not a playable environment F1F3. The looping torus offers a largely consistent object and camera workload; FurMark can keep rendering until the chosen duration or stability test ends.

Interpretation: Rotation reveals lighting and the interior of the furred ring while continuously exercising the GPU without random gameplay, camera controls, scripted NPCs or CPU-heavy world simulation. Constant movement can also make flickering, aliasing and texture issues more visible. These are sensible design consequences but no source located states them as JeGX's artistic rationale.

FurMark's 'story' is therefore mainly a performance test happening to the machine, not a drama happening to the object.

q: Why is it orange, fiery and set against checkerboards, dragons or flames?
a:
Confirmed: Screenshots and versions are not identical. A 2011 release description from JeGX explicitly mentions replacing a static background with an optional dynamic background and says those who wanted to keep their 'favourite dragon' could disable it F8. FurMark 1.8.0 had already added a heat-shimmer post-effect F7. The checkerboard and fiery backgrounds visible in different screenshots are graphic presentation, not evidence of a dragon character or a fictional volcanic location. More recent FurMark 2 presentations use an animated background; the appearance depends on test settings F2F9.

Interpretation: Hot orange/red colours visually reinforce the intense thermal test, and a patterned background supplies contrast and motion. There is no identified designer statement establishing the original colour palette's symbolism. We should not attribute every screenshot's orange tint to a precise rendering mode without identifying that version.

q: How did this almost silly object become the 'power virus'?
a:
That contrast is the unusual history. JeGX's 2007 note described a test that could overwhelm a GPU and quoted reports of exceptionally high temperatures and a PSU shutdown F1. By August 2008, independent reviewers reported AMD Catalyst driver behaviour that slowed FurMark under its original executable name, with different figures after renaming F12. Later GPU vendors added and described protective throttling, rather than treating the graphical scene as a typical game F13.

NVIDIA explicitly warned in support documentation that FurMark aims to maximise power draw well beyond real-world applications and that disabling protection mechanisms can permanently damage hardware F13. FurMark's fluffy appearance is not a safety indicator. The 'power virus' label refers to sustained workload/power behaviour; FurMark is not thereby being alleged to be malicious computer malware.

q: What do the two interlaced tori and FurMark 2 'knot' represent?
a:
Confirmed: JeGX's 1.9.0 notes introduced an optional two-torus scene with a moving camera F8. FurMark 2 adds the separate knot test alongside the familiar doughnut, with score results that should be compared within the same test rather than against donut scores F9F14.

Interpretation: Both increase visual/geometric complexity while preserving FurMark's recognisably abstract 'strange fuzzy object' identity. Torus knots are also a familiar procedural modelling subject, just as a single torus is. No source reviewed establishes a canonical story in which two doughnuts collide, the knot is a monster, or the shapes have a personality. These are alternative workloads and demo shapes, not known named characters.

q: What was the artistic point of 'Hot Like Hell' and its uneven fur?
a:
JeGX released FurMark 1.8.0 'Hot Like Hell Edition' on 2 February 2010 F7. Two striking additions were a heat post-effect and vertex displacement that allowed the fur height to change across the object (some parts could have much shorter fur). Those effects deliberately change the appearance of the object and the amount/type of shader work.

Confirmed purpose: The official release phrasing celebrated a hotter/heavier workload. Interpretation: Uneven tufts make the synthetic ring less like a uniform carpet and more like something tactile or scorched; heat haze turns a diagnostic image into a comic visual metaphor for GPU heat. There is no developer statement saying the torus itself is literally burning in a story.

It also marks a useful cultural difference from modern cinematic benchmarks: FurMark's visual polish serves its stress-test identity rather than trying to simulate a believable world.

q: Is there hidden lore behind the doughnut, and why is it still iconic?
a:
No verifiable fictional canon was found. No named protagonist, dialogue, location, motivation or ending appears in JeGX's release material reviewed here. The 'furry donut' is a distinctive benchmark object, not an edible object in a fictional story. Its enduring appeal is an interpretation: absurd visual simplicity, immediate recognisability, history with overclockers, and real effects on GPU thermals.

JeGX's 2007 writing places the purpose in the context of testing Radeon/GeForce GPUs and power supplies, not building a narrative F1. FurMark 2's decision to keep the classic doughnut while adding another geometry F9 supports its status as a project identity.

The remaining unanswered creator questions: Why did JeGX personally choose fur? Why precisely a torus? Who picked the original palette? Was the 2001 Stanford furry doughnut known to him? A dated creator interview, original source code, contemporaneous design notes or direct developer explanation would be needed. None is asserted here.

q: Who is UNIGINE, and what is the UNIGINE 2 engine?
a:
UNIGINE is a real-time 3D engine company. Its engine's roots are the open-source "frustum.org" project, started in 2002 by Alexander "Frustum" Zapryagaev, who co-founded the company with Denis Shergin (CEO) 1. The engine's first public version is listed as 0.3 on 4 May 2005, and UNIGINE's own About page says the company was established in 2005 12. In 2021 it claimed more than 250 business customers 1.

Where it is based: after a restructuring completed on 30 October 2020, UNIGINE Holding S.à r.l. in Luxembourg is the 100% parent of UNIGINE LLC (Russia). Denis Shergin is the main shareholder, and the venture firm LETA Capital is a minority shareholder. The old entity, UNIGINE Corp., was liquidated. The company then listed three offices (the Luxembourg headquarters, Tomsk and Saint Petersburg) plus remote staff across Europe and Russia 3. So Tomsk is a development office, not the headquarters. The 2013 Valley announcement quotes lead technical artist Andrey Kushner: "Living in Siberia, we wanted to show how beautiful the nature is here" 4. UNIGINE's About page says it has "more than 80" staff and that its benchmarks have "over 40 million active users" (company figures) 2.

UNIGINE 2 was released on 10 October 2015. It kept UNIGINE 1's features and moved from forward to deferred rendering, added physically based shading, geometry water, multi-layered volumetric clouds, SSRTGI and voxel-based lighting 1. The engine is C++ with C# and UnigineScript scripting 1.

q: What do typical Superposition scores look like, and who holds records?
a:
Scores depend on preset, and UNIGINE's manual says scores from different presets are not comparable and there is no overall score 5. Collected data points (all from third parties; systems differ):

  • RTX 4090, 4K Optimized: a forum user reports 39,406 on a Core i9-13900K, and 37,616 with ECC memory on 6. A Micro Center article reports 33,744 for a 4090 (its settings were not clear in the summary I saw) 7.
  • RTX 3080 Ti, 4K Optimized: forum users report 15,723 to 17,826 86.
  • Overclocking records (HWBot): on the 8K Optimized list, LN2 runs on RTX 4090 cards reach 17,657 (3885/1563 MHz) and 17,613; air and water submissions sit lower, around 15,900 to 16,800. On the 1080p Xtreme list, LN2 4090 runs reach 30,635 to 30,724 9. Tom's Hardware reported that the overclocker CENS ran an RTX 4090 at 3.825 GHz with 3D stability, validated with Superposition 8K Optimized, scoring 18,701 (his own tweet is dated 9 May 2023) 10.

HWBot standings change constantly and its pages blocked my automated fetch, so treat the figures as a snapshot from search results. A "good" score for a given card is best found in the UNIGINE global leaderboard 5. I found no authoritative GTX 1080 Ti 4K score. Not confirmed.

q: How do the stress test and VR-ready test work?
a:
UNIGINE's manual lists three test types in benchmark mode: Performance, VR Ready, and Stress 5.

  • Performance gives the actual game-like score for a preset (1080p Medium, 1080p High, 1080p Extreme, 4K Optimized, 8K Optimized, or Custom) 5.
  • VR Ready reports whether the system can run VR at the chosen quality. Its score is capped at 10,000, used only to judge VR capability, and not submitted to the leaderboards 5. Version 1.1 added a Vive Pro preset to it 5.
  • Stress is a loop over a specific time interval to check stability, available only in the Advanced and Pro editions 5.

UNIGINE describes the stress mode as "putting the GPU under a stress workload to determine the system's reliability" 5. Reviewers mostly use the Performance test: Phoronix runs the Linux OpenGL build in its test suite at 1080p High as a default profile 11.

q: Why DirectX 11 and OpenGL, not Vulkan or DX12?
a:
On Windows, Superposition offers Direct3D 11 and OpenGL; on Linux, OpenGL only (it requires OpenGL 4.5) 1213. The Linux launch reviewer hoped Vulkan would come later and a tweet suggested it was not certain 13. A 2019 reader reply confirms Linux is still OpenGL only 14.

The reason is timing. UNIGINE built Superposition on UNIGINE 2.x, whose supported APIs were DirectX 11 and OpenGL 4 1. UNIGINE 2.16 (10 October 2022) added experimental DirectX 12 and Vulkan renderers. UNIGINE wrote that "it took a while" because of "low quality of drivers and poor support from vendors at early stages" and the "industry's negative experience of porting AAA games" 15. Phoronix and 80.lv reported some features missing in that first build, and UNIGINE 2.17 lists both APIs as production-ready 16. So the engine now has newer APIs, but I found no Superposition release that uses them: version 1.1 (April 2019) is still the latest in UNIGINE's version history 5. UNIGINE has not said why. Not confirmed.

q: What are the histories of Heaven and Valley, and are they still used?
a:
Date Event Source
22 Oct 2009 Heaven 1.0 announced as the first true DX11 benchmark 17
2 Mar 2011 Heaven 2.5, plus a Professional edition 18
7 Mar 2012 Heaven 3.0, first to run on Mac 19
12 Feb 2013 Heaven 4.0: presets, GPU temperature and clock monitoring, improved SSDO, multi-GPU detection, new Advanced edition 20
14 Feb 2013 Valley 1.0, set in a forest-covered mountain valley, for Windows, Linux and OS X 421

Heaven's scene is a steampunk village on flying islands with a dragon on the central square 20. Heaven 4.0 is still the latest on UNIGINE's page, and OpenBenchmarking lists Valley profile 1.1.7 from July 2018 22. HWBot still has Heaven categories 23. Are they "still used"? Reviewers and overclockers still reference them; Wikipedia says UNIGINE benchmarks are used by Tom's Hardware, Linus Tech Tips, PC Gamer and JayzTwoCents and are part of the Phoronix Test Suite 1. I did not count current usage.

q: What about the 8K demo broadcast from space?
a: The only source is UNIGINE itself. Its 1.1 release post (12 April 2019) lists, among two years of statistics, that "the Superposition 8K demo was broadcasted from space via satellite system" 24. 80.lv repeats the sentence 25. I found no mission name, date, broadcaster or receiving network, and nothing independent. The launch coverage does confirm that UNIGINE published a 4320p (8K) 60 FPS video clip of the benchmark at release, and that 8K Optimized is a real preset 265. Whether the satellite claim means a downlink test, a trade-show feed or something else is not confirmed.

q: Which sites and test suites adopted Superposition?
a:
• Phoronix and the Phoronix Test Suite. The test profile unigine-super was created on 11 April 2017, the launch day, and the latest version listed is 1.0.8; the default configuration is 1920x1080, fullscreen, High quality, OpenGL 1112. Phoronix published a 17-card comparison the same day 12.
  • Launch coverage: Tom's Hardware, Legit Reviews, TechSpot, PC Perspective, Digital Trends, GamingOnLinux and others covered the launch 2627.
  • Ongoing use: UNIGINE's 1.1 post says Tom's Hardware, Linus Tech Tips, PC Magazine and Phoronix "use Superposition on a regular basis" 24; Wikipedia adds PC Gamer and JayzTwoCents for UNIGINE benchmarks in general 1. PC Magazine's reviews do cite it 28.
  • Overclocking: HWBot hosts Superposition leaderboards (8K Optimized, 1080p Xtreme) 9.

q: How does SSRTGI work, per UNIGINE?
a:
UNIGINE describes SSRTGI (Screen-Space Ray-Traced Global Illumination) as a set of screen-space ray tracing techniques giving real-time global illumination. It incorporates screen-space ambient occlusion, screen-space global illumination and bent normals 2930. Ordinary screen-space effects "do not treat objects as obstacles for light rays"; SSRTGI instead "provides real 180° ray tracing for each pixel in the scene with a fixed number of steps per ray to define occlusions" 30. Bent normals reduce noise and smooth shadow borders 30. The engine exposes settings for the number of rays per pixel, steps per ray, resolution and noise 29. UNIGINE's 2.5 devlog is dated 31 May 2017, and UNIGINE presented it at SIGGRAPH 2017 Real-Time Live! (post dated 1 August 2017), saying the technique was "created for Superposition Benchmark" 3031. In SDK 2.19.1 the ray distribution across the hemisphere was redesigned 32.

It is not hardware ray tracing. As a general property of screen-space methods (not a UNIGINE statement), it can only see what is on screen. I found no UNIGINE slide deck or paper with the exact sampling and denoising steps. Not confirmed.

q: What do the editions cost?
a:
From UNIGINE's current Superposition page (price table, tax not included) 33:

Edition For Price
Basic Gamer / VR user Free
Advanced Overclocker / VR user $19.95
Professional Assembly or repair shop, hardware manufacturer $495
Enterprise Company with multiple installations (unlimited seats) $7,500

Bundles including Superposition, Valley and Heaven are $29.95 (Advanced), $995 (Professional) and $14,495 (Enterprise) 33. At launch, Legit Reviews reported the Advanced edition at $19.95 26. A search summary of launch coverage suggested a $995 Professional price, which equals today's Professional bundle; I could not open that article, so I treat it as unconfirmed. The feature split (leaderboards and loop stress test from Advanced; command-line automation, CSV reports, commercial use and support from Professional) is in the manual 5.

q: How does Superposition rank among competing benchmarks in overclocking?
a: I found no ranking or participation figures that compare benchmarks, and HWBot blocked automated fetching. What the evidence does show: HWBot hosts separate Superposition categories (8K Optimized and 1080p Xtreme appear in the search results) with record-holders running RTX 4090s on liquid nitrogen 9. Tom's Hardware's coverage of the 3.825 GHz record used Superposition 8K as the 3D stability test, noting that frequency records are normally set with lighter loads like GPUPI, and that a full 3D stress test is harder 10. That implies Superposition is accepted as a demanding validation load, not that it is the most popular one. How it compares with 3DMark Time Spy or Port Royal in HWBot participation: not confirmed.

q: Who is the professor? Does he have a name, biography or identity?
a:
Canon: UNIGINE describes a lone professor who repeatedly performs dangerous experiments in an abandoned classroom. He is obsessed with spectacular inventions and discoveries and wants to prove his ideas S1. The official manual repeats that premise and, in its Game Mode instructions, also calls him 'the physicist' S2. He is absent when the player arrives, which is the reason to investigate.

Unverified: UNIGINE's product page, game-mode manual, original promotional copy and artist showcase do not name him, identify his university, provide a biography, or confirm his fate S1S2S3. 'Professor Einstein', 'Professor Tesla', 'a mad scientist named X' or 'a real scientist' would be made-up identities. Professor/physicist is the defensible description.

Character reading (interpretation): His personality is revealed through absence: his obsessive experiments and dense accumulation of notebooks and apparatus make his work, not his portrait, the protagonist.

q: Why an abandoned classroom instead of a sleek high-tech laboratory?
a:
Canon: The classroom is explicitly abandoned; the professor has repurposed it as a working laboratory S1. No UNIGINE artist statement found explains the exact artistic decision.

Observed: Official scene pictures show tall windows, old brick and timber surfaces, a classroom/lecture-hall quality, blackboards, papers and clocks alongside imposing coils, cylinders, cables and experimental equipment S3S4. The aesthetic reads as vintage academic science crossed with steampunk-like invention. 'Steampunk' is a visual description, not a separately documented story setting or official genre designation.

Interpretation: An old classroom provides visual contrast between everyday education and dangerous experimentation. Books and clutter create environmental storytelling, while tall windows and many surfaces challenge the engine with natural light, self-shadowing and material detail. We do not know why the fictional building was vacated, who owned it or whether it is in a particular country.

q: What happened immediately before the visitor arrives?
a:
Canon: The visitor reaches the site early in the morning, the professor is missing, and an unexplained loud bang was heard from the laboratory moments before S1S2. Those are the only directly documented sequence-of-events facts in the plot introduction.

Not established: Whether an explosion occurred, what device caused it, whether the professor teleported, was injured, escaped, entered a different universe or simply walked away. 'Bang' does not by itself prove any of those. Official wording frames the event as a mystery to investigate, not an already-solved tragedy.

Interpretation: This is a 'missing person / interrupted experiment' narrative hook. The apparently mundane classroom becomes ominous because its operator has disappeared just when an experiment went wrong—or at least when something made a loud noise.

q: Why does the story invoke quantum theory? Does the title 'Superposition' reveal the plot?
a:
Canon: UNIGINE directly asks visitors to investigate the mystery by looking at the professor's records and instruments, with specific reference to quantum theory S1. The title Superposition is a genuine physics term referring to systems described as combinations of possible states before a particular measurement.

Plausible reading, not confirmed plot: 'Superposition' evokes overlapping states, simultaneous possibilities, and ambiguous reality; these fit a missing scientist and an experimental catastrophe. The title is thematically apt, but no verified UNIGINE explanation identifies an exact quantum experiment or states that the professor was split into parallel copies. Such stories may be fun fan theories, not established canon.

A benchmark rendering a convincing laboratory does not itself simulate scientifically accurate quantum physics. The GPU work concerns lighting, geometry, textures and physics interactions, not a reproducible laboratory demonstration of quantum superposition S2S5.

q: What are the strange machines, rings, coils and pages?
a:
Observed: The producer's own ArtStation showcase displays a complicated large central cylindrical apparatus with protruding red components, heavy cabling, older bench instruments, metal rings, models, papers, books and classroom fittings S3. Contemporary review screenshots show optical/electrical-style equipment, gauges, a cluttered bench, furniture and chalkboards S4.

Canon is limited: The maker calls these records and instruments, relevant to inspecting the professor's work S1. In the sources reviewed, UNIGINE does not publish a part-numbered schematic assigning a fictional function to every individual machine. A visually Tesla-coil-like device is not confirmed to be 'the quantum teleporter' or 'the accident generator'.

Design interpretation: Distinct silhouettes and materials—glass, metal, paper, wood, cabling—make an environment varied enough to demonstrate modern rendering while encouraging players to ask what each device does.

q: Which items are confirmed clues and which are just props?
a:
Canon: UNIGINE specifically singles out the professor's written records and instruments as things worth inspecting S1. That is a meaningful directive from the maker. The manual calls the setting a mystery of the physicist and encourages looking in every corner S2.

But: The public manual does not provide an official itemised clue list, solved puzzle transcript, order of evidence or complete object-to-story glossary. A blackboard equation, portrait, notebook, peculiar electrical device or dartboard may carry visual meaning; without a supporting caption, readable in-game text, a developer statement or a documented puzzle solution, we cannot label it a specific plot clue.

Interpretation: The set dressing helps tell a story in the same way a film set does. The crucial research distinction is between 'looks like a clue' and 'developer confirms this reveals what happened'.

q: Can you actually be a detective and interact with the scene?
a:
Confirmed: Yes, there is a playable Game Mode, not merely a fly-through. UNIGINE's version 1.1 user manual invites players to explore, investigate the physicist's mystery, and interact with more than 900 objects S2. The listed features include physical object interactions, the ability to move and look around, and moving between game and cinematic modes. The manual maps the left mouse button to grabbing/releasing objects and describes keyboard, controller and VR controls S2.

UNIGINE also advertises mini-games. Its 2019 update notably fixed a crash when throwing darts, an unusually tangible sign that the professor's laboratory is deliberately toy-like as well as cinematic S5. Promotional artwork reinforces the emphasis on a believable, cluttered workspace S3.

Limit: Interactive objects, physics and mini-games do not independently prove a solvable hidden main quest or a canonical alternate ending. The manual's invitation is real; the answer to what solves the mystery remains unverified here.

q: How do gravity, time and lighting relate to the story?
a:
Confirmed Game Mode controls: UNIGINE documents a tweakable day/night cycle, gravity control, adjustable time scale, room lighting adjustments and the option to switch to cinematic mode S2. Those are unusually creative features for a benchmark.

Aesthetic interpretation: Moving through the room at different times and light levels can reveal previously hidden details. Turning gravity down produces floating instruments and books; a playful visual analogue to a physics experiment and a useful demonstration of the engine's physical interactions. It is not confirmed that changing gravity unlocks a plot revelation or that time control lets you undo the bang.

The technological purpose is clearer: the same setting can show changing direct/screen-space illumination and many dynamic objects S6. Keep the gameplay/physics controls separate from the title's quantum metaphor.

q: Is there an official ending, proof of where he went, or a solution to the mystery?
a:
The honest result is unresolved. UNIGINE's marketing copy announces the mystery and its manual encourages solving it, but the primary material reviewed does not disclose an explicit final cutscene, named culprit, device activation, answer or official ending S1S2S3. The available changelog describes software features and bug fixes, not story chapters or narrative updates S5.

This does not prove no player has ever worked something out in the executable; we did not complete an interactive playthrough or examine every object. It means a claimed ending needs evidence before being presented as fact. A reproducible walkthrough or developer comment could fill that gap.

Current story boundary: We know the setup (missing professor, bang, experiments, records), not a definitive cause or resolution.

q: Is the laboratory based on Tesla, Einstein or a specific science-fiction tradition?
a:
Visually: The workshop includes experimental electrical machines, coils, drawings and old-school physics teaching furnishings S3S4. Those can reasonably evoke the historical laboratory imagery associated with Nikola Tesla, early twentieth-century physics, vintage classrooms and steampunk design.

Fact check: The sources consulted contain no confirmed UNIGINE statement that the unnamed professor is Tesla, Einstein or a historical person, that the setting represents an identifiable university, or that a specific film/game inspired the art. A picture of a celebrated scientist on the wall—if positively identified—would still be a portrait, not proof that the professor is that person.

The larger published context is clear: Superposition follows UNIGINE's outdoor Sanctuary, Tropics, Heaven and Valley demos, but chooses an enclosed, detail-rich lab mystery to show off its UNIGINE 2 engine, dynamic SSRTGI lighting and interactive physics S6S7. That change of stage helps give this benchmark a character beyond its score.

q: How are Time Spy and Steel Nomad scored, and what do they render?
a:
Time Spy (14 July 2016) is a DirectX 12 benchmark with two graphics tests and one CPU test. UL publishes exact score calculations 1:

  • Graphics score = 164 × 2 / (1/FPS1 + 1/FPS2): a scaled harmonic mean of the two graphics-test average frame rates. Using a harmonic mean prevents one unusually fast scene from masking a slow scene.
  • CPU score = 298 × FPS_CPU3, based on the heaviest of three 10-second CPU-test stages.
  • Overall Time Spy = 1 / (0.85/graphics score + 0.15/CPU score). It is a weighted harmonic mean, not 85% of one score simply added to 15% of the other. Low CPU scores can therefore pull the total down even when the GPU is fast.
  • Time Spy tests use a custom, multithreaded engine with a DirectX 12 rendering pipeline including asynchronous compute, explicit multi-adapter support, and compute/graphics work submitted through queues. The engine uses occlusion culling and other modern techniques; its 2016 technical explanation was prepared with feedback from competing GPU vendors 23. It is a synthetic gaming-style workload, not an actual game benchmark.

Steel Nomad (21 May 2024) is a single GPU graphics test, with no CPU test. Its overall and graphics scores are identical: score = average graphics FPS × 100 4. For example, 45.00 FPS means 4,500 points. Standard Steel Nomad renders 3840 × 2160; Steel Nomad Light is 2560 × 1440, a separate test with its own scale and leaderboard 56. UL's engine documentation describes computer-generated terrain/grass with compute-shader distribution, moving ray-marched volumetric clouds, contact shadows, screen-space reflections with cubemap fallbacks, depth-of-field, bloom, XeGTAO ambient occlusion and temporal antialiasing 7. Standard Steel Nomad is not a ray-tracing benchmark: ray marching volumetric clouds and screen-space effects do not make it a hardware DXR/path-tracing test.

Why these distinctions matter. Neither a Time Spy total and a Time Spy Graphics score, nor Time Spy and Steel Nomad, are interchangeable. Match exact test name, test version, resolution, API, driver and hardware before comparing results. Extreme and Light editions are distinct tests. A CPU bottleneck can still invalidate a GPU-only score if command submission is too slow 58.

q: How big is the user base and result database, and who holds the records?
a:
There are dated, sourceable scale measurements, but not a reliable public running total of unique users or all accepted results:

  • March 2003: Futuremark said 3DMark03 had been downloaded more than 2.5 million times in its first month 9. Downloads are not unique users or purchases.
  • September 2003: Futuremark said its combined benchmark products had over 2 million registered users and more than 10 million submitted results 10. This was not a 3DMark-only figure.
  • 2016: Futuremark described 3DMark as used by millions of gamers and hundreds of review sites, without a precise unique-user count 11.
  • May 2024: UL reported almost 48 million Time Spy result submissions since 2016, and said the average Time Spy score had roughly tripled 12. Submissions are not a count of unique computers, people or paid licences.
  • 2025: UL said hundreds of thousands of people had run Solar Bay before Solar Bay Extreme arrived 13. This is a different population and timeframe.

Records are test-specific and fluid. UL maintains the official 3DMark Hall of Fame and per-test rankings 14. That is where current official 3DMark/VRMark/legacy records must be checked; a result posted by a third-party site is not automatically an official record. UL validates eligibility and requires approved drivers, publicly available hardware and benchmark-specific restrictions, including CPU-based NVIDIA PhysX for Vantage record submissions 1415. Enthusiasts overclock and sometimes use exotic cooling; those records should not be used as everyday factory-speed purchase recommendations.

Unanswered after research: no independently audited, up-to-date count for all unique 3DMark users, total lifetime submissions across every test, total paid licences, or a stable list of 'the record holder'. Listing a username without the date and the exact test would become stale.

q: What happened in the 3DMark03 NVIDIA driver controversy and smartphone delistings?
a:
The 2003 dispute unfolded in stages rather than ending with one settled verdict. After suspicious performance changes, Futuremark audited NVIDIA Detonator FX drivers and published a report dated 23 May 2003 identifying eight detection mechanisms; changing benchmark code without changing the intended graphics workload stopped those mechanisms. Futuremark released 3DMark03 build 330 to prevent the detectors from distorting scores 1617. Independent contemporary reporting described up to 24.1% score impact in some configurations, along with altered output 18.

On 2 June 2003, Futuremark and NVIDIA issued a joint statement reclassifying the driver behaviour as application-specific optimisation rather than 'cheating' 19. That reversal does not erase the technical audit. In a September 2003 interview Futuremark said the substance of the audit was still correct, but the terminology was too contentious 20. ATI was also scrutinised: ATI acknowledged optimising two shaders in 3DMark03; contemporary reporting put the overall boost around 1.9% and recorded ATI's claim of mathematical equivalence 21. Futuremark subsequently published formal benchmark optimisation guidelines on 23 September 2003, separating general-purpose improvements from workload-specific manipulation 22. This is an historically significant case about benchmark trust, not simply 'NVIDIA cheated and got caught'.

The problem returned on smartphones. UL's rules prohibit a device from detecting the 3DMark app and secretly increasing clocks or switching performance profiles only for it. UL compares a normal executable with an otherwise identical, renamed one, and delists stock models with proven application-dependent behaviour 23. Its published examples include some Samsung Galaxy S4/Note 3 Android 4.3 builds, HTC One/One Mini, Oppo Find X/F7, Huawei P20/P20 Pro/Nova 3/Honor Play, and, as listed in 2026, RedMagic 11 Pro/11 Pro+. Some older Samsung devices became eligible again with a software update. A delisted phone's owner is not accused of personally cheating 23. The question is whether benchmarked performance represents ordinary applications, including thermal and power policies.

q: Why did Time Spy's asynchronous compute implementation cause controversy?
a:
The debate arose during the DirectX 11-to-12 transition, when GPUs differed in their ability to overlap compute work and graphics rendering. AMD marketed dedicated async compute capability, while NVIDIA Maxwell and Pascal architectural behaviour differed. Media and enthusiasts asked whether a test that benefits one architecture was 'fair' and whether disabling async changed results 2425.

Futuremark's 19 July 2016 technical response is unusually precise 3. Time Spy submits work into a graphics/direct queue and a compute queue; around 10–20% of the GPU workload per frame was described as asynchronous compute in contemporary testing 25. The benchmark implementation is the same across GPU vendors. Actual concurrent execution is a driver/hardware scheduling decision, not an API guarantee. Advanced/Professional users can disable async in a custom run: the compute work moves into the direct queue, preserving the visual workload 3. Therefore a custom no-async run is a diagnostic, not a directly comparable official preset score.

PCWorld compared Radeon and GeForce cards with async enabled and disabled. In that review the tested AMD cards lost substantially more performance without async than many NVIDIA Maxwell cards, while a GTX 1070 also showed benefit 26. PC Perspective published its own per-GPU experiments 25. These observations describe those specific 2016 cards/drivers and tests, not a universal result for every generation.

Conclusion: the documented architecture-sensitive behaviour was real, but it is not proof that Time Spy secretly changed work depending on vendor. Whether a synthetic workload predicts an individual game depends on that game's own compute/graphics scheduling, engine, resolution and GPU.

q: Which feature tests exist and when did they arrive?
a:
A feature test isolates a particular graphics capability or technology, unlike a full benchmark combining many game-like effects. UL's official update chronology gives this timeline 27; current tests and editions are listed in its support guide 28.

First release Test or capability What it investigates
2015 API Overhead CPU/API draw-call overhead; later added Vulkan (2017)
2019 NVIDIA DLSS Upscaled vs non-DLSS performance and image quality; DLSS 2 support in 2020, DLSS 3 support in 2022, later updates
2019 PCI Express Host-to-GPU PCIe transfer bandwidth
2019 Variable Rate Shading (VRS) Performance and image-quality effect of shading different image regions at different rates
2020 DirectX Raytracing Isolated DXR ray-tracing workload, rather than hybrid rasterisation plus ray tracing
2021 Mesh Shader Geometry-processing efficiency with mesh shaders
2021 Sampler Feedback Texture sampling/streaming technique on compatible DX12 Ultimate GPUs
2022 Intel XeSS Upscaling and image quality using supported hardware
2023 AMD FSR Upscaling and image-quality effects (UL describes FSR 2.2)
2022/2023 Speed Way / Solar Bay These are full benchmarks, not feature tests; respectively DX12 Ultimate ray tracing and cross-platform mobile/desktop ray tracing

UL has also shipped CPU Profile, Storage Benchmark and DirectStorage tests, but those are CPU/storage/component tests, not the same list of GPU-rendering feature tests 2829. Availability depends on platform and licence: many feature tests need the paid Advanced or Professional Edition on Windows. Test scores from unlike features should not be ranked as if they measured the same thing.

q: What is the history of 3DMark mobile benchmarks?
a:
The mobile branch reflects changes in phone GPU APIs and power efficiency:

Date Family Technology and significance
2013 Ice Storm / Ice Storm Extreme Cross-platform baseline: DirectX 11 feature level 9 on Windows tablets, OpenGL ES 2.0 on phones 30
27 July 2015 Sling Shot Android OpenGL ES 3.0/3.1, multiple render targets, instancing, volumetric lighting; new high-end phone workload 31
15 October 2015 Sling Shot iOS Released on iPhone/iPad, allowing comparable OpenGL ES 3.0 testing 32
15 October 2020 Wild Life Cross-platform Apple/Android/Windows modern game-like scene, quick score and prolonged stability/thermal stress test 33
2021 Wild Life Extreme Heavier workload for faster mobile devices 2734
14 August 2023 Solar Bay Mobile-class Vulkan ray queries and cross-platform ray-traced rendering on compatible devices; iOS addition followed in September 2023 3536
21 May 2024 Steel Nomad Light 1440p non-ray-traced, cross-platform; includes Android and iOS versions 1236
20 August 2025 Solar Bay Extreme Substantially more complex ray-traced reflections, glass and soft shadows; Windows, Windows-on-Arm, macOS, Android and iOS 13

UL stopped supporting Ice Storm on 14 January 2020, because it had become too easy for modern devices 30. On phones, the key question is often not peak short-run FPS but sustained performance after heat builds up; UL recommends the 20-minute stress tests when reviewing smartphones and thin laptops 34.

Cross-platform scores are designed for comparable workloads, but different rendering APIs, driver implementations, system thermals and power limits mean equal scores do not prove architectural equivalence. Only compare the same test (and ideally the same version) across systems, and distinguish Vulkan/Metal/DirectX where relevant 2937.

q: What did 3DMark cost, and what do Steam sales tell us?
a:
The prices below are historical US-dollar list prices or stated publisher offers, not today's Australian pricing and not lifetime revenue 1038394041.

  • 11 February 2003: 3DMark03 was a free public download, with US39.95 *  * paidindividualeditionand *  * US250 corporate licence 38.
  • 12 September 2003: Futuremark cut the paid 3DMark03/PCMark2002 individual versions to US$19.95 10.
  • 5 February 2013: new 3DMark Basic was free, Advanced US24.99 * *,Professional *  * US995 (contemporary publisher-sourced coverage) 39.
  • July 2016: Time Spy was added free to the basic tests; Advanced rose from US24.99toUS29.99 after 23 July; pre-existing buyers could choose a separate Time Spy feature upgrade 40.
  • 12 October 2022: Speed Way brought Advanced's advertised price from US29.99toUS34.99, with an optional US$4.99 upgrade for eligible existing owners 41.
  • Steam page inspected November 2026: the US-price page displayed US$29.99 normal price and separate optional DLC prices; regional prices, temporary sales and licence bundles can differ 42. This shows that an old price announcement is not a dependable present-day price.

Edition naming note (2026): UL's current reviewers' guide calls the free tier 3DMark Demo, the consumer paid tier 3DMark, and the commercial tier 3DMark for Enterprise; historical announcements used Basic, Advanced and Professional. These names have evolved, so a 2013 price list is not a current commercial licence offer 34.

Business model: 2013 onward, 3DMark shifted away from issuing a completely new standalone suite for each DirectX generation. UL keeps adding free tests, paid upgrades and some separate DLC; business use requires the licensed Professional/enterprise route, not simply owning the consumer Steam version 274143.

What about success? A Steam product page exposes reviews and its catalogue, but does not reveal independently auditable gross sales, net revenue, margins or total paying customers. SteamSpy/third-party owner and revenue estimates are model-derived rather than receipts. No actual lifetime Steam revenue or unit sales could be confirmed. Claims that Steam popularity proves precise revenue would be false precision.

q: What else did Futuremark make, and what was the Vantage PhysX dispute?
a:
Beyond 3DMark, Futuremark/UL created PCMark (whole-PC, office/applications, storage and platform benchmarking), VRMark (VR performance and headset readiness), Peacekeeper (web-browser performance), Powermark (laptop battery runtime), Servermark (enterprise/VDI/media-transcoding), Video2000, and other specialised products 44. UL's archived history dates Peacekeeper to March 2009 and its cross-device update to 2011; Peacekeeper later ended support. PCMark evolved into separate desktop and mobile-oriented versions rather than simply measuring game graphics 45. These are siblings, not merely earlier versions of 3DMark.

The 2008 3DMark Vantage PhysX argument was about what a supposedly CPU result means when a GPU can run the physics simulation. Vantage's CPU tests included a physics workload using PhysX. With supported NVIDIA hardware/driver, portions could execute on the GPU, dramatically raising the CPU sub-score and indirectly the overall score 4647. NVIDIA argued that it was legitimate acceleration of the test rather than changing test code 47; critics objected that the resulting number stopped being an apples-to-apples CPU comparison. This is different from 2003's driver-detection audit.

The enduring resolution is pragmatic: UL's official Vantage Hall of Fame requires NVIDIA PhysX to run on the CPU for comparable record scores 14. A historical Vantage score with GPU PhysX enabled should not be compared uncritically with one using CPU-only physics.

q: How does the Benchmark Development Program work, and who participates?
a:
UL's Benchmark Development Program (BDP) brings hardware and software companies into test design, technical review and early feedback. The public programme page describes access to benchmark workload/source-level details, feedback from specifications through release candidates, and private Developer Edition licensing 48. UL states that every partner in the same tier pays equal fees and that one company cannot simply pay extra to dominate the outcome; this is UL's own description, not an independent audit.

UL explicitly names AMD, Intel, NVIDIA and Microsoft as participants in developing Time Spy, including the async-compute implementation 3. Port Royal's engine documentation names AMD, Intel and NVIDIA as contributors and says Microsoft was especially closely involved in DXR implementation 49. Speed Way's announcement also credits AMD, Intel, NVIDIA and other partners 50.

Why it is both valuable and complicated: competing vendors can identify incompatibilities before a benchmark launches and help make a test representative of real APIs. But the same companies have commercial interests in ranking well. The safeguards are common workloads, documented formulae, vendor-neutral code paths, published rules and validation of results 222348. Membership alone does not guarantee an unbiased final test; that depends on independent reproducibility. The current complete paying membership roster and any confidential vote/decision records were not publicly verified.

q: How were Port Royal and Speed Way received, and do their results match games?
a:
Port Royal launched 8 January 2019 at 2560 × 1440, with a hybrid rasterisation + DirectX Raytracing scene, including ray-traced reflections and shadows 5152. It was an early way to compare GPUs capable of Microsoft's DXR technology. Because it had no CPU test, it primarily targeted the GPU; CPU command-list throughput can still become a limitation 53. At launch RTX hardware was the central consumer use case. German testing site ComputerBase found that within the RTX card family some broad relative performance patterns resembled those in Battlefield V, but also warned that synthetic benchmarks are not substitutes for actual game measurements; its alternative rasterisation comparison was not an adequate like-for-like image-quality comparison 54.

Speed Way launched 12 October 2022 as a more modern DirectX 12 Ultimate workload. It uses DXR tier 1.1 reflections and global illumination, mesh shaders, and the 2560 × 1440 scene; the publisher also provided an interactive scene and VS comparison mode 5055. Unlike Time Spy or Steel Nomad, it demands ray-tracing-capable hardware. Its specifications and sponsor/product placement were transparent in the launch announcement. It received attention as a demanding modern feature showcase, but that is not evidence that one Speed Way point predicts a certain frame rate in Cyberpunk or any other game.

UL does provide statistical game-FPS estimates for selected combinations of games, resolution and settings, by measuring correlations with benchmark results (examples include Time Spy Graphics against Fortnite, Apex Legends and Red Dead Redemption 2) 56. This does not give a universal Port Royal/Speed Way-to-game FPS conversion. Correlations can shift with ray-tracing implementation, driver changes, CPU limits, memory, upscalers, frame generation, power settings, thermal behaviour and game patches.

Practical reading: use Speed Way for DX12 Ultimate/ray-tracing-capable GPU comparison, Port Royal for its older DXR hybrid test, Steel Nomad for non-ray-traced native 4K, Time Spy Graphics for broader older DX12 comparisons, and real gameplay benchmarks for a particular game's expected FPS. Comparisons across the benchmark families' point totals are invalid 295155.

q: How are Time Spy and Steel Nomad scored, and what do they render?
a:
Time Spy. Two graphics tests (2560x1440) and a CPU test. The overall score is a weighted harmonic mean: (W_g + W_c) / (W_g / S_g + W_c / S_c), with the graphics weight 0.85 and the CPU weight 0.15 1. The graphics score is the harmonic mean of the two tests' average frame rates times a scaling constant, which brings it in line with traditional 3DMark levels; the CPU score derives from simulation time per frame 1. A harmonic mean means a weak CPU or GPU drags the total down more than an arithmetic mean would 1.

Steel Nomad. Rendering resolution 3840 x 2160, DirectX 12 feature level 12 or Vulkan 1.1, one graphics test and no CPU test 2. The overall score equals the graphics score, which is the average frame rate times 100 3. Speed Way uses the same rule: score = average FPS x 100 4.

What Steel Nomad renders (UL's "engine" page) 5: opaque objects with deferred rendering into a G-buffer with PBR material parameters, shading in linear HDR; order-independent transparency; decals; reflections and diffuse global illumination sampled from probes spread around the scene; GPU-simulated particles (compute shaders); grass in compute shaders with distance-based level of detail; a dynamic ray-marched volumetric cloud sky; screen-space contact shadows; screen-space reflections with a cube-map fallback; heat distortion from particles; compute-shader FFT bloom (blur, streaks, anamorphic flare, lenticular halo); a three-pass froxel volume illumination for fog; scatter-as-gather depth of field; and XeGTAO ambient occlusion (ultra quality in compute shaders in Steel Nomad, high quality in pixel shaders in Light) 5. Steel Nomad uses asynchronous compute to overlap the first volume-illumination pass with other passes; Light does not, and also has no volume illumination 5. It is explicitly non-ray-traced 6. Version history: 1.0, launch version, and no later version 7.

q: How big is 3DMark's user base, and who holds records?
a:
UL gives few total figures. Hard numbers from UL: Time Spy had "almost 48 million" submitted results by May 2024 6; the Android app had "more than 100,000 downloads in its first week" (April 2013) and the iOS app 50,000 downloads in two weeks (September 2013) 8; UL describes the 3DMark Hall of Fame as the home of world-record scores 9. A third-party download page claims "25 years, 50M+ results" but I could not trace that to UL, so I treat it as unconfirmed 10. I found no UL total for all results or for active users.

Records: cached Hall of Fame pages show Port Royal's top entries in the high 40,000s on RTX 5090 systems (for example 47,311 on an RTX 5090 with a Core i9-14900KS at rank 85 in one snapshot), and an old Time Spy snapshot headed by multi-GPU rigs 9. The pages carry a notice about turbulence and the snapshots are of different dates, so these are not current standings. HWBot and the Hall of Fame both hold records; I did not reconcile them. Not confirmed.

q: The 3DMark03 driver scandal and the smartphone delistings
a:
May 2003. An ExtremeTech investigation of Nvidia's drivers prompted a Futuremark audit 11. On Friday 23 May 2003, Futuremark published a seven-page audit of Detonator FX 44.03 and 43.51 drivers listing eight instances where it believed Nvidia modified drivers unfairly; renaming the benchmark executable lowered scores in certain tests 1112. Futuremark's patch 330 stops the drivers recognising the benchmark; it measured the GeForce FX 5900 Ultra dropping about 24% with it, versus under 2% for ATI's Radeon 9800 Pro 12. The Register (27 May 2003) reported ATI also admitted tweaks: renaming the executable cut Game Test 4 by 8% and the total by just under 2% (ATI said it was an optimization of the water and sky shaders, "mathematically and functionally identical", and promised to remove it) 11. Weeks later Futuremark reversed course: it said Nvidia's approach was an "application specific optimization" rather than a cheat, but still said the rules were broken, and did not reinstate the original results; a joint statement called for clear industry rules for benchmarks 13.

Phones. On 7 September 2018 UL delisted the Huawei P20 Pro, Nova 3 and Honor Play (and the P20 based on AnandTech's testing). UL compared the public 3DMark app with a private build that is not available to manufacturers: public-app scores were up to 47% higher with identical tests, meaning the phones recognised the app by name. Delisted devices appear unranked, without scores 14. Other delistings reported: OPPO's Find X and F7 (2018) and a 2013 sweep of HTC and Samsung Android devices 15; and in April 2020 MediaTek-based phones from Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, Sony and Realme 16.

q: The Time Spy asynchronous compute controversy
a:
In July 2016 a forum post on Overclock.net argued Time Spy's async compute use fit Nvidia's architecture better than AMD's: in DOOM and Ashes of the Singularity the Fury X beat a GTX 1070, but not in Time Spy 17. PC Perspective explained the issue and noted the causes were unknown (driver maturity, optimization differences) 17.

Futuremark replied on 19 July 2016 with a detailed post. Its main points: Time Spy was developed with input from AMD, Intel, Microsoft, NVIDIA and others in the Benchmark Development Program, in development for nearly two years; vendors spent weeks in the office, downloaded daily source drops hundreds of times, and exchanged "around one thousand emails" on it; the engine uses two queues, DIRECT and COMPUTE, regardless of the hardware; "the implementation is the same regardless of the underlying hardware" with no vendor-specific optimizations; and whether COMPUTE-queue work runs in parallel or serial "is ultimately the decision of the underlying driver" because DirectX 12 only lets an application permit parallel execution 18. The post shows GPUView traces for the GTX 970, Fury and GTX 1080 with async compute on and off, and the compute work items: particle simulation, light culling and tiling, environment reflections, HBAO and unshadowed surface illumination 18. Futuremark's stated principle is that 3DMark predicts games in general, not absolute theoretical maximums 18. Forum claims that Nvidia's driver disables async on pre-Pascal cards, or that Time Spy's version is "preemption based", are unconfirmed forum claims 19.

q: Which feature tests exist, and when did they arrive?
a:
From UL's About-page timeline and release notes 820:

Date Feature test
March 2015 API Overhead, "the world's first DirectX 12 API performance test" (Vulkan added March 2017; Android Vulkan August 2017)
June 2016 Stress tests added (loop runs to check stability)
February 2019 NVIDIA DLSS feature test (DLSS 2 and three quality modes added September 2020; DLSS 3 and Frame Generation October 2022)

q: The mobile tests
a: UL's timeline gives: 3DMark for Android in April 2013 (100,000+ downloads in the first week), iOS in September 2013 (50,000 in two weeks), Windows RT in October 2013 8. Ice Storm and Ice Storm Extreme were released in 2013 and support ended on 14 January 2020 (Ice Storm used OpenGL ES 2.0 on mobile) 23.
